failure_modes: State-space dependence: the same system yields different entropies under different state definitions or binnings, so values are comparable only within one state space
Finite-sample bias: entropy estimated from few samples is biased low
Reading low entropy as 'good order' without asking what constrains it
gloss: The average surprise of a distribution: how many bits it takes to predict an outcome
invariants: H is non-negative and zero only for a distribution concentrated on one state
H is maximal for the uniform distribution over the state space
H depends only on the probabilities, not on what the states are or how they are ordered
mechanism: For a discrete distribution P = {p_i} over states i, H(P) = -sum_i p_i log p_i, the expected self-information -log p_i of an outcome. Rare outcomes carry much information, likely ones little. H is maximal (log m for m states) when all states are equally likely and zero when all probability sits on one state. Applied to a system's possible configurations, high H means many weakly constrained configurations (variability, flexibility, exploration) and low H means strong constraints (regularity, coordination). Use log base 2 to measure in bits.
preconditions: A discrete state space has been defined and outcomes can be counted into it
